name: Levothyroxine: timing and other medicines
headline: Levothyroxine: why timing and other medicines matter, as the NHS describes
summary: The NHS says levothyroxine replaces a missing thyroid hormone, taken at a consistent time on an empty stomach, apart from some foods and medicines.
keyPoints: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid that replaces a hormone the body is not making enough of.
The NHS says it is taken at the same time each day, on an empty stomach, before the first meal, any caffeinated drink or other medicines.
MedlinePlus, a US source, says calcium, iron, multivitamins and some antacids are best spaced apart from thyroid medicine.
The NHS says regular blood tests check hormone levels, first while the right amount is found and then usually once a year.
The NHS says treatment is usually lifelong, and both the NHS and MedlinePlus say not to stop without medical advice.

body.heading: What does levothyroxine replace?
body.body: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid, also called hypothyroidism. In an underactive thyroid the gland does not make enough of them. The NHS says an underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. It explains that the tablets simply replace a hormone that is missing, which is why they do not usually cause side effects. The NHS says diagnosis uses a thyroid function test, a blood test that measures TSH and thyroxine (T4). The NHS says combining levothyroxine with a second thyroid hormone, T3, is not routinely used because there is not enough evidence that it works better than levothyroxine alone. A high TSH level together with a low T4 level could mean the thyroid is underactive.

body.heading: Why does the NHS say to take it at a consistent time?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine is usually taken once a day, at the same time each day. It also says the tablet is taken on an empty stomach, before the first meal of the day, any caffeinated drink or any other medicine. MedlinePlus, a US source, says thyroid medicine works best on an empty stomach. Some NHS trust leaflets note that people choose morning or bedtime, so the choice of time is something to settle with the prescriber or pharmacist. The NHS also advises a forgotten tablet is taken when remembered unless the next one is nearly due, and that two are not taken together to make up.

body.heading: How can food, coffee and other medicines affect it?
body.body: A systematic review in the US National Library of Medicine's PubMed Central database examined how levothyroxine interacts with food and dietary supplements. This is why the NHS wording about an empty stomach, before food, caffeinated drinks and other medicines matters. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists fibre supplements, calcium, iron, multivitamins, aluminium hydroxide antacids and bile-acid binding medicines as products to space apart from thyroid hormone. An NHS trust leaflet also names calcium and iron as able to reduce absorption. Biotin, a vitamin found in some supplements, can affect thyroid blood test results, so clinicians ask about supplements. Which products, and what spacing, apply to one person is a question for a pharmacist or the prescriber, using the leaflet in the pack.

body.heading: Why are regular blood tests needed?
body.body: The NHS says people have regular blood tests at first, until the right amount of levothyroxine has been reached. Once the amount is right, it says a blood test is usually done once a year to monitor hormone levels. These tests measure thyroid hormone levels, including TSH. MedlinePlus, a US source, also says hormone levels are checked at the start and then at least once a year. The NHS says pregnancy brings further tests and that the amount of levothyroxine is likely to need changing. The NHS also says symptoms may ease soon in some people, while others do not notice improvement for several months.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping?
body.body: The NHS says to keep taking the medicine unless advised to stop. It says an underactive thyroid is a lifelong condition, so people usually need levothyroxine for the rest of their lives. MedlinePlus, a US source, says to keep taking it even when feeling well and not to stop without talking to a doctor. The NHS says that left untreated, an underactive thyroid can lead to complications such as heart disease, goitre and pregnancy problems. A pharmacist or GP is the usual route for questions about changes.

body.heading: What side effects can happen, and who can advise?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine does not usually have side effects, because the tablets replace a missing hormone. It says most side effects happen when the amount is too high, and they often improve once the amount is changed. Effects listed include trouble sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating, hair loss, diarrhoea and being sick. Serious reactions are rare, and the NHS lists an allergic reaction and thyroid crisis, which can cause a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, or dizziness. These are emergencies, so the route is 999. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists chest pain, an irregular heartbeat, seizures and confusion as warning signs after taking too much thyroid medicine, and advises emergency care. For side effects that bother a person or do not go away, the NHS says to speak to a doctor or pharmacist. If more than the prescribed amount has been taken, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible, and to call NHS 111 if one cannot be reached or it was done on purpose.
